html:
Hadramaut is a region in the south of the Arabian peninsula, in today's eastern Yemen, centred on a long, deep valley, the Wadi Hadramaut, cut into a high desert plateau. On the map it appears off and on from 323 BCE to 1700 CE.

In ancient times it was one of the kingdoms of South Arabia, with its capital at Shabwa. It controlled the lands where frankincense grew, inland and along the coast of today's Dhofar, and it shipped incense through its port of Qana. It was a rival and sometimes ally of Saba and Qataban, and it was rich from the incense trade. Hadramaut swallowed Qataban, but around 300 CE it was itself conquered by the Himyarite kingdom.

After Islam came in the 600s the valley kept its own character. From the 900s the town of Tarim became a centre of Islamic learning, especially for the Ba Alawi, a family of sayyids, descendants of the Prophet Muhammad. Its towns built tall mud brick tower houses; Shibam, with buildings up to eight storeys high, is sometimes called the Manhattan of the desert.

Hadramis were great travellers. Merchants and scholars from the valley settled around the Indian Ocean, in East Africa, India and especially Southeast Asia, where they helped spread Islam and often grew rich; many sent money home. This was part of the wider world of Indian Ocean trade.

In modern times the region was divided between the Kathiri and Qu'aiti sultanates, under British protection from the late 1800s as part of the Aden Protectorate. In 1967 it became part of South Yemen, and since 1990 it has been part of a united Yemen.
sum: Hadramaut is a region in the south of the Arabian peninsula, in today's eastern Yemen, centred on a long, deep valley, the Wadi Hadramaut, cut into a high desert plateau. On the map it appears off and on from 323 BCE to 1700 CE.
